statement: Prove that $\tan2\theta=\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^{2}\theta}$, and hence solve $\tan2\theta=1$ for $0\le\theta<\pi$.
solution:
$\tan2\theta=\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{\cos2\theta}=\dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta-\sin^{2}\theta}=\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^{2}\theta}$ (dividing by $\cos^{2}\theta$). Setting $\tan2\theta=1$ gives $2\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi$, so $\theta=\frac{\pi}{8}+\frac{k\pi}{2}$. In $[0,\pi)$ the solutions are $\theta=\frac{\pi}{8}$ and $\theta=\frac{5\pi}{8}$.
